Looking at this step by step:

**1. Outside view / Base rate:**
The series shows: 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 6, 7, 6, 6, 11. Mean ≈ 5.6, with typical week-to-week moves of 0-2 points. The series had been stable around 6-7 in late August before the 11.0 spike. That +5 jump is unusual — roughly 2.5x the typical weekly change.

**2. Inside view:**
The Daily Kos article (Sep 9) reveals the 11.0 was **not** a standard generic ballot question — YouGov asked voters using the **names of actual candidates** in their district, which tends to produce higher Democratic margins due to incumbent name recognition. Other polling averages as of Sep 10 show D+5.7 (RealClearPolling), D+6.4 (DDHQ), D+6.6 (Nate Silver) — all well below 11. The Economist/YouGov tracker itself was at 6-7 throughout August. If the Sep 15 wave returns to the standard generic ballot question, significant mean reversion toward the 6-8 range is likely. I estimate this methodology effect is worth roughly -3 to -4 points off the 11.0, but some genuine Democratic momentum may have occurred, so not full reversion.

**3. Pre-mortem:**
If wrong, most likely because either (a) the 11.0 was genuinely from the standard generic ballot question and reflects a real shift — in which case Sep 15 could print 9-11, or (b) I underestimated the reversion and it drops back to 6. The Daily Kos article's explicit statement about named candidates makes (a) less likely, but I should keep the mean above the polling average to hedge.

**4. Calibration:**
Week-to-week changes have SD ≈ 1.9 (including the +5 anomaly). The margin of error on the difference is roughly ±5 at 95% confidence with n≈1,500. Combined uncertainty about methodology and sampling gives SD ≈ 2.5, producing a 68% interval of roughly 5-10.
